paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. Seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy, often as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, and the EEG shows suppression-burst or hypsarrhythmia. Patients have severe to profound developmental delay and intellectual disability with abnormal muscle tone. Non-neural features vary between patients and include cleft palate, joint contractures, pes equinovarus, omphalocele, skeletal abnormalities and dysmorphic facial features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish (2 families), Iranian and Brazilian origin. Seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all patients. In the 10 patients whose early history was available, onset was in the first month. At onset, seizures were mainly myoclonic seizures (n = 5) or epileptic spasms (n = 6). Seven of 8 patients who had an EEG during the neonatal period showed a suppression-burst or burst-attenuation pattern. Two patients whose first EEG was recorded later showed hypsarrhythmia. Antiepileptic drugs eventually controlled seizures in 6 patients, and in 5 of these, seizures were controlled for long periods after vigabatrin was added. All living patients had severe psychomotor delay, and intellectual disability was profound in all who could be assessed. Head circumference was normal in all patients but one. The authors described markedly increased muscle tone (spasticity, tetraparesis, segmental hypertonia, dystonia) as a core feature, and patients often also had axial hypotonia. Brain MRI was normal in 5 patients. One patient had a hypoplastic corpus callosum with progressive cerebral and cerebellar atrophy, and another had mild cerebral atrophy with ventricular enlargement at 6 years of age. Among the non-neurologic features, 7 patients had cleft palate, 6 had joint contractures, 5 had pes equinovarus and 4 had scoliosis. Three patients had dysmorphic facial features with no clear shared elements. Four patients died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: In the Egyptian family reported by Chatron et al. (2020), 2 sibs had omphalocele, which reproduced the phenotype of the Gad1-null mouse. The sister also had polyhydramnios, jejunal atresia, cleft soft palate and a branchial fistula. She had multiple joint contractures with camptodactyly and rocker-bottom feet, and dysmorphic features that included hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, microretrognathia, low-set abnormal ears, skin hemangiomas, neck and axillary webbing, and clitoral enlargement. She died at 2 years of age. Her brother had omphalocele, bilateral talipes equinovarus and arthrogryposis, and he died at 4 years of age. In one of the Turkish families, the proband had cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, pes equinovarus, flexion contractures, neck and axillary webbing and facial dysmorphism, with epileptic spasms and hypsarrhythmia from 1 month of age. His older brother was born at 29 weeks' gestation with cleft palate, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease and pes equinovarus, and he died of sepsis on day 9.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry. The clinical table listed the parents as consanguineous in 5 families. All patients were born at term after a normal pregnancy. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures with or without impaired awareness. Two patients also had epileptic spasms, 4 had focal non-motor seizures and 5 had bilateral motor seizures. The EEG at onset showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Seizures were controlled with medication in 3 patients and were drug-resistant in 3. Brain MRI was normal in all but 2 patients, one with slight ventricular enlargement and one with moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay. Intellectual disability was severe in 5 and moderate in 1. Only 1 patient developed simple speech, and this patient remained seizure-free on medication. The other patients remained severely impaired even when their seizures were controlled. Five patients had reduced muscle tone or strength. In 4 this was severe enough to cause limited head control and inability to sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four patients had slight dysmorphic facial features, and only 1 had cleft palate. That patient also had congenital bilateral hip dislocation with shallow acetabulum, talipes equinovarus and hearing impairment. Other features without clear common elements included high myopia, hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs and scoliosis. Metabolic workups were normal.

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) performed whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing in 11 patients with DEE89 from 6 consanguineous families. In every family, a rare homozygous GAD1 variant was the only likely pathogenic variant retained. Sanger sequencing confirmed that the variants segregated with the disease in each family. In 4 families, the variants were predicted to truncate the protein. These were a splice site mutation (c.1414-1G-C), a 5-bp frameshift deletion (c.812_816delTTAAG), and a nonsense mutation (R531X) shared by an Iranian and a Turkish family. In lymphoblastoid cells from the parents in the family with the splice site variant, cDNA analysis showed no normal mRNA product and 3 aberrant isoforms. An Egyptian family carried an in-frame 3-bp deletion (c.695_697delAGA, K232del). In a cell-free system, the K232del protein was expressed at levels comparable to wildtype, but the authors noted that this assay bypasses splicing. A Brazilian family carried a missense mutation (E509K) at a highly conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain. The authors noted that the gnomAD pRec score for GAD1 (0.934) was consistent with intolerance to biallelic loss-of-function variants.

paragraphs.text: In a Sudanese boy with DEE89 born to consanguineous parents, Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.1040C-T transition in the GAD1 gene, resulting in a thr347-to-met (T347M) substitution in the PLP-binding domain. In silico analysis predicted broken hydrogen bonds in that domain. The variant was reported twice in the heterozygous state in gnomAD. The boy had epileptic spasms with hypsarrhythmia from 2 months of age, severe hypotonia, dysphagia and dysmorphic features. His heterozygous sister had a different neurodevelopmental condition without seizures.

paragraphs.text: In an Egyptian girl with DEE89 born to first-cousin parents, Neuray et al. (2020) identified a homozygous c.87C-G transversion in the GAD1 gene, resulting in a tyr29-to-ter (Y29X) substitution. The variant was absent from the population databases queried and was predicted to cause nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. The girl had refractory seizures, severe hypotonia, cleft palate, congenital bilateral hip dislocation, talipes equinovarus and hearing impairment. A similarly affected sib died without genetic testing.
